newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank extends Bangladesh jute credit deadline.
newsitem.headline: World Bank extends Bangladesh jute credit deadline.

text.p: The World Bank has extended by six months the deadline for disbursing a $250 million credit for revamping Bangladesh's loss-making jute sector, government officials said on Tuesday.
They said the extension, effective January 1, 1997, followed a request by the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who took over in June 1996.
The decision was communicated to the government recently in a letter from Marilou Uy, chief of the World Bank's Private Sector Development and Finance Division for South Asia, the officials said.
The letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, said the closing date of the Jute Sector Adjustment Credit (JSAC) was extended until June 30, 1997.
The new government had sought an extension of one year. The letter said that if progress in implementing the programme was satisfactory the bank would consider one more extension
The credit agreement was signed between the International Development Association (IDA), a soft-loan subsidiary of the World Bank, and the Bangladesh government in February 1994.

The conditions included "elimination of excess capacity (looms) in the jute industry by closing nine of the 29 public sector mills and downsizing two large public mills, retrenchment of about 20,000 employees in the state-run mills, privatisation of at least 18 of the remaining 20 public mills, retraining for retrenched workers under a social safety net programme," one official said.

Accordingly, the government shut down four public sector jute mills, downsized one large mill, sacked about 12,000 workers and abolished the state-run Bangladesh Jute Corporation. It also issued bonds against the liabilities of the commercial banks of the closed mills.

The IDA disbursed $50 million in a first instalment in April 1994 but the remaining instalments have since remained suspended because the then government of prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia had failed to fulfil all the conditionalities.
The letter said the World Bank would make an overall assessment of progress under the JSAC in early June.

The government, which spends about $500 million annually on subsidies to state-owned companies, recently signed an agreement to transfer the loss-making Purbachal Jute Industries to a foreign company.
